idiom_name: Celery task message: app.send_task / Task.delay with a task name and JSON payload
implementation_notes: Python command messages are tasks: app.send_task('orders.reserve_stock', args=[...], kwargs={...}) publishes a task message that names the operation - a command in the EIP sense - and a worker deserializes it, looks up the registered task and executes it, with routing (queue, routing_key), retries, time limits and expiry supplied by Celery/Kombu rather than by application code. The in-process reduction is a dict payload plus a handler dict keyed by an operation string, or singledispatch on typed command classes, which is what a hand-rolled command bus looks like. Celery is justified when delivery, retries and horizontal scale-out are needed; a plain dispatch table suffices inside one process.
pitfalls: The task name is a wire contract: renaming the function without a name= alias (or moving the module) breaks messages already queued and disables worker discovery.
Celery delivers at least once and retries by default, so the task body must be idempotent or deduplicate on a key taken from the arguments.
Only JSON-serializable arguments may be sent; passing model instances or connections raises at publish time, and DisableSubmitRetry-style switches hide the failure in the broker.
